opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fundamental questions there is, and I'd put it alongside the big questions in physics. I've always thought of information as perhaps the most fundamental unit of the universe, more fundamental than energy or matter in some sense. If you take that view seriously, the universe starts to look like an informational system. Not necessarily a simulation in the video game sense, but something that's computable, at least in principle.

If that's the case, then P versus NP isn't just a question in computer science or mathematics. It becomes a question about physics, about what's actually tractable in the real world. What can nature compute efficiently, and what can we, as information-processing systems inside that universe, hope to model?

What's been fascinating to me with things like AlphaGo and AlphaFold is that we seem to be able to solve problems that look, on the surface, completely intractable. The search space of Go is enormous, more positions than there are atoms in the universe. Protein folding has a combinatorial explosion of possible configurations, Levinthal's paradox. Yet nature folds proteins in milliseconds, and our systems can now predict those structures very accurately.

So my conjecture, and it's only a conjecture, is that many natural systems have structure. They aren't random. They've been shaped by evolutionary processes, physical constraints, or some kind of selection over time, and that structure creates a lower-dimensional manifold you can learn. If you can learn a good model of that structure, you can guide your search efficiently through what would otherwise be an exponentially large space. You don't brute-force it.

That suggests classical systems, like neural networks running on ordinary computers, may be able to do much more than we thought, perhaps even model some things people assumed needed quantum computers. That doesn't resolve P versus NP formally, of course. But it might mean the set of problems that matter in the natural world, the ones with that kind of learnable structure, is far more tractable than worst-case complexity theory would suggest.

For me that's one of the deepest and most exciting things about AI. It's a tool for advancing science, but it's also a way of probing these fundamental questions about the nature of reality and computation. I'd love to see AI help us understand what the true boundaries of the knowable and the computable really are.

r001.rationale: The response calls information more fundamental than energy or matter and describes the universe as an informational system, but it does not say that information, energy, and matter can be converted into one another.

r002.rationale: The response links the view of the universe as an informational system to framing P versus NP as a physics question about what nature can compute efficiently.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually one of the deepest questions there is, and I've thought about it a lot. My view, as you say, is that information may be the most fundamental thing in the universe, perhaps more fundamental than matter or energy. If that's right, then physics itself is in some sense a computational process, and questions like P versus NP stop being purely abstract mathematical puzzles and become questions about the nature of reality.

The way I think about it is this. P versus NP is really asking: are problems whose solutions are easy to check also easy to solve? And when you look at the natural world, it's full of structure. Protein folding is a nice example, because that's something we worked on directly with AlphaFold. In principle, the space of possible conformations is astronomically large, Levinthal's paradox and all that. But proteins fold in milliseconds. Nature isn't brute-forcing it. There's structure there, there are regularities, and if you can learn those regularities, the problem becomes tractable in practice even if it's hard in the worst case.

So my intuition is that P is probably not equal to NP in the formal sense, I'd agree with most complexity theorists on that. But I think the more interesting question for someone building AI is a slightly different one: how much of the universe, how much of what we actually care about, lies in this space of problems that have exploitable structure? And my hunch is, a lot of it. Almost everything we'd call science is the discovery of that structure. Physics is compressible. The laws are simple relative to the phenomena they generate. That's an incredible fact about the world, and it's not obvious it had to be that way.

So in a way, you could think of AI, and deep learning in particular, as a kind of empirical probe into this question. We're finding out, domain by domain, which hard-looking problems actually have learnable structure underneath them. Games, protein structure, materials, maybe eventually things like fusion or weather. And each time it works, it tells you something about the computational character of that part of reality.

There's a speculative version of this that I find quite beautiful, which is that if information is primary, then the universe is, in some sense, the computation, and the question of what's tractable is really a question about what kinds of things the universe can bring into being. I wouldn't claim that as a rigorous position. But it's the kind of thing that, if we eventually build systems capable of real scientific insight, I'd love to point them at. Because I suspect the answer will be stranger and more interesting than either a simple yes or no.

r001.rationale: The response calls information potentially more fundamental than matter or energy, but does not say that information, energy, and matter can be converted into one another.

r002.rationale: It connects information as fundamental and the universe as a computational process to treating P versus NP as a question about the nature of reality.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes P versus NP feel like a question about the structure of reality, rather than just an abstract mathematical puzzle. If information is fundamental, then the distinction between finding a solution and checking a solution may tell us something quite deep about what the universe allows us to compute.

Take a problem where, once someone gives you an answer, you can efficiently verify that it’s correct. Does that mean there must also be an efficient way to discover that answer? That’s the essence of P versus NP. My intuition is that P probably doesn’t equal NP—that there is a fundamental difference between those two things. But intuition is obviously not a proof.

The connection I find fascinating is with physics. Can a physical process give us a computational shortcut that our mathematical models don’t capture? And if someone proposes one, have they really solved the problem, or have they hidden the difficulty in preparing the system, measuring the answer, or requiring extraordinary precision?

So I’d want to understand those questions together: what can be computed, what resources it takes, and what physical laws permit. Viewing information as fundamental gives you a way to connect them. It doesn’t, by itself, settle P versus NP.

r001.rationale: The response discusses information as fundamental but does not say information, energy, and matter can be converted into one another.

r002.rationale: It connects P versus NP to physics and physical laws, grounding that connection in the view that information is fundamental and computation is part of reality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes me wonder whether computational complexity is telling us something very deep about the structure of reality. If information is fundamental, then the distinction between finding a solution and checking a solution may be more than a mathematical curiosity. It may reflect a fundamental constraint on what can happen in the universe.

With P versus NP, you can have a problem where, once someone gives you an answer, it’s relatively easy to verify, but finding that answer seems extraordinarily difficult. My intuition is that P probably doesn’t equal NP. But that’s an intuition, not a proof, and you have to be very careful about drawing mathematical conclusions from a view about physics.

What fascinates me is whether there’s a deeper principle connecting the two. Does the universe impose limits on computation that help explain why certain problems are hard? And could understanding those limits tell us something about the universe itself? I think that’s a beautiful meeting point between computer science, physics, and philosophy.

r002.rationale: It connects P versus NP to the universe’s computational limits and asks whether those limits reveal something about reality, framing the question as a meeting point of computer science and physics.
